title: Must and have (got) to
subtitle: must be / has got to be
summary: Use must for rules, reminders and conclusions, and learn when have to or have got to is the only natural choice.

lesson.heading: Rules, regulations and warnings
lesson.text: We use must and must not in formal rules and regulations and in warnings.

examples.text: Bookings **must be made** at least seven days before departure.
The government **must not be allowed** to appoint judges.

lesson.heading: Loose arrangements and reminders
lesson.text: In spoken English we often use must and mustn't to propose a future arrangement without making detailed plans. We also use I must ... to remind ourselves to do something.

examples.text: We **mustn't** leave it so long next time.
**I must** charge my phone. I meant to do it yesterday, but I forgot.

lesson.heading: Drawing conclusions
lesson.text: For a conclusion about the past we use must + have + past participle; about now, must be + -ing; about the future, must be going to or must be + -ing; about a present situation, must be (or, informally, have (got) to be).

examples.text: That's not Clara's car. She **must have borrowed** it from her parents.
I can't hear a noise. You **must be imagining** things.
'What are all those workmen doing?' 'I think they **must be going to** dig up the road.'
Their goalkeeper **has got to be** at least two metres tall!

lesson.heading: must have to and must have had to
lesson.text: We use must have to to conclude something from what we know about a present situation, and must have had to to conclude something about a past situation.

examples.text: I can't access the database. You **must have to** put in a password.
Matt wasn't at home when I went round. He **must have had to** go out unexpectedly.

lesson.note: We can't say ~~must've got to~~, but must've had to is fine.

lesson.heading: Questions
lesson.text: In questions that hope for or expect a negative answer we prefer have (got) to; must is used in formal contexts. We also use have to in questions that imply a criticism, stressing have.

examples.text: **Do we have to** answer all the questions?
examples.note: or Have we got to ...?; formally Must we ...?

examples.text: **Do you have to** play your trumpet here? It's deafening!
examples.note: formally Must you play ...?; some people find must old-fashioned here

lesson.heading: When have to beats have got to
rows: I often **have to** work at the weekend to get everything done.
with frequency adverbs: always, never, normally, rarely, sometimes
When **did you have to** give it back?
past simple questions - not ~~When had you got to give it back?~~
We **didn't have to** wait too long for an answer.
past simple negatives - not ~~We hadn't got to wait ...~~
Motorists **will have to** wait until next year to use the bridge.
after another modal verb - not ~~will have got to wait~~
I need new shoes, and they'**ve got to** be blue.
if have is contracted, got must be included - not ~~they've to be~~
lesson.note: Otherwise have got to is often preferred in informal speech.

lesson.text: Keep the two conclusions apart: *You must have to put in a password* = I conclude it is necessary now; *He must have had to go out* = I conclude it was necessary then.

exercises.prompt: When I left my laptop on the train I thought I'd never see it again. But someone ___ it and handed it in to the lost property office.
exercises.explanation: A conclusion about something that happened in the past: must + have + past participle.

exercises.prompt: Luisa owns a big car and a yacht. She ___ incredibly rich.
exercises.explanation: A conclusion about a present situation: must be (or, informally, has got to be).

exercises.prompt: *A:* Everyone's going into the hall. *B:* The meeting ___ soon. Let's go.
exercises.explanation: A conclusion about the near future: must be + -ing, or must be going to + infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence with the version that uses have (got) to.

pairs.left: It is necessary to do all of this photocopying before lunchtime.
pairs.right: All of this photocopying has got to be done before lunchtime.

pairs.left: It is rarely necessary to ask Hannah to tidy her room.
pairs.right: Hannah rarely has to be asked to tidy her room.

pairs.left: It wasn't necessary for me to go to the hospital after all.
pairs.right: I didn't have to go to the hospital after all.

pairs.left: Was it necessary for Ben to go alone?
pairs.right: Did Ben have to go alone?

pairs.left: It may be necessary to cancel our holiday because my mother is ill.
pairs.right: We may have to cancel our holiday because my mother is ill.

exercises.prompt: Without things like washing machines and dishwashers our grandparents ___ much harder in the kitchen than we do today.
exercises.explanation: We conclude that it was necessary for them: must have had to + infinitive.

exercises.prompt: *A:* I wonder how you get past security. *B:* I suppose you ___ some form of ID.
exercises.explanation: We conclude from a present situation that something is necessary: must have to + infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite 'It is sometimes necessary for Adam to start work at 6:30.' using have to.
exercises.answer: Adam sometimes has to start work at 6:30.
exercises.explanation: With frequency adverbs we prefer have to rather than have got to.

exercises.statement: The door's very stiff, and I always have got to pull it very hard to shut it.
exercises.explanation: The door's very stiff, and I always have to pull it very hard to shut it. With frequency adverbs we use have to.

exercises.statement: My neighbour's always saying, 'Have you to bang the door so hard?'
exercises.explanation: 'Do you have to bang the door so hard?' Questions that imply criticism take do you have to (formally Must you ...?).

exercises.prompt: None of the windows and doors were damaged, so someone very small ___ through the tiny window in the kitchen.
exercises.explanation: A conclusion about what was necessary in the past: must have had to + infinitive.

exercises.prompt: I think the burglars ___, perhaps when the postman came.
exercises.explanation: A conclusion about a past event, in the passive: must have been + past participle.

exercises.prompt: I suppose I ___ get a burglar alarm, too.
exercises.explanation: Two modal verbs can't follow each other, so may must becomes may have to.
